rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse illustrates God’s guidance and support for believers and His abandonment of others; Al-Ālūsī says it is therefore not coordinated with the preceding statement.
rows.anchor: بيان لتسديد المؤمنين إذ كان وليهم وخذلان غيرهم ولذا لم يعطف

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: An alternative takes the story as evidence for the preceding claim that unbelievers’ allies are the Taghut, while the following passage supports God’s guardianship of believers.
rows.anchor: وقيل : إستشهاد على ما ذكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story comes first to pair it with its referent, to foreground its striking independent interest, and to avoid dispersing the later, more detailed sequence.
rows.anchor: وبدأ به لرعاية الاقتران بينه وبين مدلوله ولإستقلاله بأمر عجيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham’s call to truth and defeat of the unbeliever’s argument also show God guiding believers through His guardianship.
rows.anchor: فإن ما يحكى عنه من الدعوة إلى الحق وإدحاض حجة الكافرين من آثار ولايته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The interrogative hamza denies the apparent negation and affirms the denied proposition; the audience is asked to marvel at a story whose fame makes it virtually undeniable.
rows.anchor: وهمزة الإستفهام لإنكار النفي وتقرير المنفي والجمهور على أن في الكلام معنى التعجب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address means, “Have you seen or heard of this unbeliever?” His extraordinary challenge should reassure the Prophet: God aided Abraham and defeated the chief of the tyrants.
rows.anchor: فلتكن في الغاية القصوى من تحقق ما ذكرته لك من ولايتي للمؤمنين وعدمها للكافرين ولتطب نفسك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The person who disputed with Abraham was Nimrod son of Canaan son of Senjarib, described as the first tyrant to claim divinity.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالموصول نمروذ بن كنعان بن سنجاريب وهو أول من تجبر وإدعى الربوبية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The text calls the encounter a disputation even though Nimrod argued falsely, because his false argument was presented as if it were a real proof.
rows.anchor: وإنما أطلق على ما وقع لفظ المحاجة وإن كانت مجادلة بالباطل لإيرادها موردها

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: One report places the dispute after Abraham broke the idols and before Nimrod cast him into the fire.
rows.anchor: قبل إلقائه في النار وهو المروي عن مقاتل

rows.speaker: جعفر الصادق
rows.claim: A report from Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq places the dispute after Abraham was cast into the fire and it became cool and safe for him.
rows.anchor: وهو المروي عن جعفر الصادق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling God Abraham’s Lord honors Abraham and signals from the outset that God, as his guardian, will support him in the dispute.
rows.anchor: وفي التعرض لعنوان الربوبية مع الإضافة إلى ضميره عليه الصلاة والسلام تشريف له وإيذان من أول الأمر بتأييد وليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause means “because God granted him kingship,” with an omitted causal lām; it is not an object of purpose because the agents differ.
rows.anchor: أي لأن آتاه الله تعالى ذلك فالكلام على حذف اللام وهو مطرد في أن وإن وليس هناك مفعول لأجله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On one causal reading, God’s grant of kingship caused Nimrod’s arrogance and insolence, which led him to dispute.
rows.anchor: إما أن إيتاء الملك حمله على ذلك لأنه أورثه الكبر والبطر فنشأت المحاجة عنهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second causal reading is ironic: Nimrod disputed despite having reason to thank God for the kingship He had granted.
rows.anchor: وإما أنه من باب العكس في الكلام بمعنى أنه وضع المحاجة وضع الشكر إذ كان من حقه أن يشكر على ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another parsing treats “gave him” as temporal, with or without an implied noun: Nimrod disputed when God granted him kingship.
rows.anchor: واقعا موقع الظرف بدون تقدير أو بتقدير مضاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Critics object that the grant preceded the dispute and that a temporal adverb normally requires an explicit verbal noun; defenders invoke an extended period and the temporal use of مصدرية ما.
rows.anchor: وأورد عليه أن المحاجة لم تقع وقت إيتاء الملك بل الإيتاء سابق عليها وبأن النحاة نصوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī prefers the causal construction because it is agreed and avoids the strained temporal analyses and disputed grammatical exceptions.
rows.anchor: والحق أن التعليل لما أمكن وهو متفق عليه خال عما يقال لا ينبغي أن يعدل عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse supports that God can grant kingship to an unbeliever; restricting the grant to wealth, servants, and followers, or calling it a test, does not remove the theological problem.
rows.anchor: والآية حجة على من منع إيتاء الله الملك لكافر وحملها على إيتاء الله تعالى ما غلب به وتسلط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some avoid attributing kingship to Nimrod by making the pronoun in “gave him” refer to Abraham instead.
rows.anchor: بعضهم جعل ضمير ( آتاه ) لإبراهيم عليه السلام

rows.speaker: أبو قاسم البلخي
rows.claim: Abū al-Qāsim al-Balkhī takes the recipient of the kingship as Abraham, connecting the claim to the covenant’s exclusion of wrongdoers and to Abraham’s descendants receiving immense kingship.
rows.anchor: وهو المحكي عن أبي قاسم البلخي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī rejects the Abraham reading as contrary to the apparent sense and early transmitted exegesis; Abraham then had no rule, authority, or command.
rows.anchor: ولا يخفى أنه خلاف المنساق إلى الذهن وخلاف التفسير المأثور عن السلف الصالح

rows.speaker: بعض الإمامية
rows.claim: Some Imāmīs distinguish prohibited kingship, which invests someone with command and obligatory obedience, from Nimrod’s coercive power, wealth, and influence.
rows.anchor: وذهب بعض الإمامية إلى أن الملك الذي لا يؤتيه الله للكافر هو ما كان بتمليك الأمر والنهي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī says the Imāmī argument comes close to the truth in assigning true kingship to Abraham, though he detects doctrinal misdirection and an insinuation against the Companions.
rows.anchor: بل الذي أوتي ذلك في الحقيقة إبراهيم عليه الصلاة والسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording shifts from a pronoun to God’s explicit name, a noteworthy choice in this context.
rows.anchor: وفي العدول عن الإضمار إلى الإظهار في هذا المقام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The temporal “when Abraham said” can attach to “disputed”; it has also been proposed as a substitute for “gave him,” though that assumes the Abraham reading.
rows.anchor: إذ قال إبراهيم ( ظرف لحاج

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān objects to making this a substitute for the grant because the two time expressions refer to different times.
rows.anchor: واعترضه أبو حيان بأن الظرفين مختلفان إذ وقت إيتائه الملك ليس وقت إبراهيم عليه السلام

rows.speaker: ما روي
rows.claim: A report says Abraham spoke these words while imprisoned for breaking the idols, after Nimrod asked who was Lord of the one calling people to the truth.
rows.anchor: فانه على ما روى قاله أن سجن لكسره الأصنام وإثر قول نمروذ له وقد كان أوتي قبل الملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One common approach sees Abraham switch to a clearer proof after Nimrod’s objection; a second says he switches only the example, from life and death to sunrise.
rows.anchor: وفيه دليل على جواز انتقال المجادل من حجة إلى أخرى أوضح منها وهي مسألة متنازع فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the second approach, Abraham’s first claim concerned creating and annihilating possible things; life and death were examples, replaced by the clearer sun example.
rows.anchor: هو في المثال كأنه قال

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: Al-Imām argues that an apparent objection heard by an audience must be answered immediately, or confusion remains and an infallible messenger seems to leave a challenge unanswered.
rows.anchor: قال الإمام : والإشكال عليهما

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: Al-Imām says silence after the opponent’s challenge diminishes the messenger’s standing and makes him appear insignificant.
rows.anchor: والثان أنه لما أورد المبطل ذلك السؤال كان ترك المحق الكلام عليه والتنبيه على ضعفه مما يوجب سقوط وقع الرسول

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: Al-Imām says the sun proof is weaker: humans cannot create life, but they can move bodies, so a powerful celestial being might move the heavens.
rows.anchor: والثالث أنه وإن كان الانتقال من دليل إلى آخر أو من مثال إلى غيره لكنه يجب أن يكون المنتقل إليه

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: Al-Imām objects that Nimrod could claim to cause sunrise and challenge Abraham’s God to make it rise from the west; answering that challenge could force a miracle and displace the proof.
rows.anchor: والرابع أن المارد لما لم يستح من معارضة الإحياء

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: Al-Imām adds that even if the sun rose from the west, that new event would become the proof, leaving the original sun argument wasted.
rows.anchor: وأيضا فبتقدير أن يحصل طلوع الشمس من المغرب يكون الدليل على وجود الصانع هو هذا الطلوع لا الطلوع الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first-person yāʾ in “my Lord” is read with fatḥ or omitted.
rows.anchor: بفتح الياء وقرئ بحذفها وأراد عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham meant that God creates life and death in bodies.
rows.anchor: وأراد عليه السلام يحي ويميت يخلق الحياة والموت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nimrod meant something else: according to a report, he brought two men, killed one, spared the other, and claimed that he gave life and death.
rows.anchor: فقد روي عنه أنه أتى برجلين فقتل أحدهما

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: Al-Imām’s preferred account treats both statements as one proof: if life and death are direct, Nimrod cannot establish that claim; if mediated by celestial motions, humans lack power over those motions.
rows.anchor: فالحق أن هذا ليس دليلا آخر ولا مثالا بل هو من تتمة الدليل الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī says Nimrod’s claim was so plainly false that Abraham could leave it unanswered without confusing the audience or diminishing his authority.
rows.anchor: أما أولا فلأن الشبهة إذا كانت في غاية السقوط ونهاية البطلان بحيث لا يكاد يخفى حالها

rows.speaker: رُوي
rows.claim: One report says Abraham did answer Nimrod, pointing out that Nimrod made the living dead but did not make the dead alive.
rows.anchor: روى أنه ما انتقل حتى بين للمارد فساد قوله

rows.speaker: الصادق
rows.claim: Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq reports Abraham challenging Nimrod to revive the man he had killed if his claim were true.
rows.anchor: وعن الصادق رضي الله تعالى عنه أنه قال له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an omits that refutation because Nimrod’s claim is manifestly false.
rows.anchor: لكن لم يقص الله تعالى ذلك الإلزام علينا في الكتاب اكتفاءا بظهور الفساد جدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī rejects al-Imām’s claim that the sun proof is less clear, calling the opposite nearly undeniable.
rows.anchor: وأما ثانيا فلأنه من الواضح أن المتنقل اليه أوضح في المقصود من المتنقل عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The possible westward-sun objection also applies to al-Imām’s account of celestial motion; proposed explanations that the fire miracle silenced Nimrod or God made him forget are offered, but the latter is weak.
rows.anchor: وقد أجابوا عن عدم قول اللعين ذلك بأن المحاجة كانت بعد خلاصه من النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham’s proof rests on the self-evident need for a mover: Nimrod cannot be the mover, so if he claims to cause this motion, let him make the sun rise from the west.
rows.anchor: بل الجواب أنه عليه السلام أستدل بأنه لابد للحركة المخصوصة والمتحرك بها من محرك لان حاجة المتحرك في الحركة إلى المحرك بديهية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī says al-Imām’s celestial-motion reconstruction is not indicated by the verse or Nimrod’s stated claim, so it should not be imposed on the text.
rows.anchor: وأما رابعا فلأن ما اختاره لا تدل عليه الآية الكريمة بوجه وليس في كلام الكافر سوى دعواه الإحياء والإماتة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī relays the possibility that Nimrod did not claim to be the world’s sole god; he may have believed in delegated gods, as some Sabians attributed creation and governance to planets, and imagined such power could be delegated to an earthly being.
rows.anchor: من أن المارد لما كان مجوزا لتعدد الآلهة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham exposes Nimrod’s inability to hold delegated creative power by invoking his necessary knowledge that he was born after not existing and therefore depends on a creator.
rows.anchor: أراد إبراهيم عليه السلام أن ينبه على قصوره عن هذه الرتبة وفساد رأيه من جهة علمه الضرورى بأنه مولود أحدث بعد أن لم يكن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham does not state the whole doctrine of divine uniqueness; he hints that life and death are kinds of creation and annihilation, and a creator of every possibility must be wholly outside possibility, since multiplicity entails dependence.
rows.anchor: على أنه لوح اليه من حيث أنه لا فرق بين الايجاد والاعدام نوعين هما الاحياء والاماتة والقادر على إيجاد كل ممكن وإعدامه يلزمه أن يكون خارجا عن الممكنات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nimrod’s reply suggests that an agent may depend on a creator for initial existence yet act independently thereafter, a position Al-Ālūsī attributes to deficient theologians.
rows.anchor: كما عند بعض القاصرين من المتكلمين مفوضا إليه بعد إيجاده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nimrod contradicts himself: if he independently governs and creates, he is not delegated power by the Creator and cannot be free of dependence even briefly; sparing someone is not creating life.
rows.anchor: وهذا قد خفى على الأذكياء فضلا عن الاغبياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham makes the same point through the sun: the one responsible for its continued motion must also be responsible for its origination; Nimrod cannot assign the two to different agents.
rows.anchor: فألزمه الخليل عليه السلام بأن القادر لا يفترق بالنسبة اليه الدوام والابتداء فان الله تعالى يأتى بالشمس من المشرق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The challenge exposes Nimrod’s mistaken division of origination and continuation before the audience; the exchange is one integrated proof, not a switch to another argument or a clearer example.
rows.anchor: مظهرا لدى السامعين ما كان عسى أن يغبى على البعض فهذا كلام وارد على الخطابة والبرهان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second statement names God directly rather than saying “my Lord,” countering Nimrod’s “I” and asserting God’s lordship over Abraham and Nimrod.
rows.anchor: وإنما أتى في الجملة الثانية بالاسم الكريم ولم يؤت بعنوان الربوبية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording rises from the earthly dispute to the heavens; “indeed” strengthens the assertion, and the imperative is a challenge that demonstrates incapacity.
rows.anchor: ففيه ترق عما في تلك الجملة مالترقى من الأرض إلى السماء وهو في هذا المقام حسن التأكيد بأن والامر للتعجيز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first fa signals that the sun argument follows from the preceding claim; the sense is that if Nimrod misunderstood or argued sophistically, this removes the confusion.
rows.anchor: والفاء الاولى للايذان بتعلق ما بعدها بما قبلها والمعنى إذا ادعيت الإحياء والإماتة لله تعالى وأخطأت أنت في الفهم أو غالطت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bāʾ is transitive, and both occurrences of min mark the starting point of motion.
rows.anchor: في الموضعين لابتداء الغاية متعلقة بما تقدمها من الفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, each min phrase can be attached to an omitted circumstantial description meaning “subjugated” or “obedient.”
rows.anchor: وقيل : متعلقة بمحذوف وقع حالا أي مسخرة أو منقادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Buhita” means he was overcome, left speechless, and bewildered when the proof prevailed.
rows.anchor: أي غلب وصار مبهوتا منقطعا عن الكلام متحيرا لاستيلاء الحجة عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reading buhita, with bāʾ open and hāʾ rounded, and bahita, with hāʾ kasra, are intransitive forms.
rows.anchor: وقرئ بهت بفتح الباء وضم الهاء وبهت بفتح الأولى وكسر الثانية وهما لغتان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With both first syllables open, the verb may be intransitive with “the one who disbelieved” as subject, or transitive with Abraham as subject and the unbeliever as object.
rows.anchor: بفتحهما فيجوز أن يكون لازما أيضا

rows.speaker: الكيا
rows.claim: Al-Kiyā takes the verse to show that disputing in religion is permitted, even though Nimrod’s particular disputation was disbelief.
rows.anchor: قال الكيا : وفى الآية دليل على جواز المحاجة في الدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God does not guide wrongdoers to paths of truth as He guided His allies; another reported interpretation is that He does not guide them to Paradise on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: إلى مناهج الحق كما هدى أولياءه وقيل : لا يهديهم إلى طريق الجنة يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse resumes the account of God’s power and might by declaring His encompassing knowledge of the entire world, including believers’ faith and unbelievers’ disbelief.
rows.anchor: استئناف لبيان سعة علمه سبحانه وإحاطته بجميع ما فى العالم الذى من جملته إيمان من آمن وكفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s all-encompassing knowledge reinforces the warning, indicates that He is living, and shows that Jesus’s knowledge of some unseen matters does not attain the divine attributes.
rows.anchor: وفى بيان ذلك تربية للوعيد وإشارة إلى دليل كونه حيا وتنبيه على أن الوقوف على بعض المغيبات كما وقع لعيسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Earth” and “heaven” together mean the whole universe.
rows.anchor: والمراد من الأرض والسماء العالم بأسره

rows.speaker: الكثير
rows.claim: Many treat the paired terms as a metaphor that names parts while intending the whole.
rows.anchor: وجعله الكثير مجازا من إطلاق الجزء وإرادة الكل

rows.speaker: من قال
rows.claim: Those who deny a whole-part relation in “all” unless it has genuine composition and can perish with a part classify the expression as metonymy rather than metaphor.
rows.anchor: بناءا على اشتراط التركيب الحقيقى وزوال ذلك الكل بزوال ذلك الجزء جعل المذكور كناية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earth precedes heaven to focus attention on earthly affairs and the warning to the misguided; the later mention of heaven also creates an ascent in expression.
rows.anchor: وتقديم الأرض على السماء إظهارا للاعتناء بشأن أحوال أهلها واهتماما بما يشير إلى وعيد ذوى الضلالة منهم وليكون ذكر السماء بعد من باب العروج

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One explanation says the negation particle is placed between earth and heaven for this rhetorical ordering.
rows.anchor: قيل : ولذا وسط حرف النفى بينهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The negative clause is the predicate of inna, and repeating the predication strengthens the assertion.
rows.anchor: والجملة المنفية خبر لإن وتكرير الاسناد لتقوية الحكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “in the earth” modifies an omitted adjective of “thing”; negation makes the phrase universal, whatever the kind of containment.
rows.anchor: وقع صفة لشئ مؤكدة لعمومه المستفاد من وقوعه فى سياق النقى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saying that nothing is hidden from God is more emphatic than merely saying that He knows it.
rows.anchor: والتعبير بعدم الخفاء أبلغ من التعبير بالعالم

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ also allows the locative phrase to attach directly to “is hidden.”
rows.anchor: وجوز أبو البقاء الظرف بيخفى

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān’s preferred parsing supplies an omitted “make him” and coordinates “a messenger” with “teach him.”
rows.anchor: وهو الذي اختاره أبو حيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another analysis supplies an omitted verb of saying and coordinates Jesus’s “I was sent” with “teach him”; this works if the coordination is with an independent “teach” clause.
rows.anchor: أي ويقول عيسى أرسلت رسولا

rows.speaker: التفتازاني
rows.claim: Al-Taftāzānī objects when the saying is coordinated with “gives you glad tidings” or “creates,” since that joins clauses without a proper link.
rows.anchor: فقد طعن فيه العلامة التفتازاني بأنه يكون التقدير إن الله يبشرك أو إن الله يخلق ما يشاء ويقول عيسى

rows.speaker: البحر
rows.claim: Al-Baḥr calls the saying analysis weak in all forms because it requires ellipsing both the saying and its complement when the accusative circumstantial noun suffices.
rows.anchor: وفي البحر : إن هذا الوجه مطلقا ضعيف

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some instead coordinate the word with the preceding circumstantial descriptions, understanding it as “a messenger speaking thus”; the person shift is then harmless.
rows.anchor: واختار بعضهم عطفه على الاحوال المتقدمة مضمنا معنى النطق فلا يضر كونها في حكم الغيبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the main analyses, “messenger” is an adjective like “grateful” or “patient”; the faʿūl pattern here has the sense of mufʿil.
rows.anchor: والرسول على سائر التقادير صفة كشكور وصبور وفعول هنا بمعنى مفعل

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ allows “messenger” as a verbal noun, cites a poetic line using the word, and would coordinate it with “the Book” as a thing taught.
rows.anchor: كما قال أبو البقاء مثله في قوله الشاعر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī rejects the verbal-noun analysis: the adjectival sense is more immediate, and “teaching a message” is not found in Arabic usage.
rows.anchor: بعيد لفظا ومعنى أما الأول فلأن المتبادر الوصفية لا المصدرية وأما ثانيا فلأن تعليم الرسالة مما لا يكاد يوجد في كلامهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase may modify “messenger” directly or describe him through an omitted phrase, meaning a messenger sent to all the Children of Israel.
rows.anchor: والظرف إما متعلق برسولا أو بمحذوف وقع صفة له أي رسولا كائنا إلى بني إسرائيل أي كلهم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A reported explanation says Israel is singled out to indicate Jesus’s particular commission or to answer a Jewish claim that he was sent to others.
rows.anchor: قيل : وتخصيصهم بالذكر للإيذان بخصوص بعثته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī doubts that Jews made the claim that Jesus was sent to non-Jews; it is absent from the well-known books he has seen.
rows.anchor: ولي في نسبة هذا الزعم لبعض اليهود تردد وليس ذلك في الكتب المشهورة

rows.speaker: أكثر اليهود
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī says most Jews accuse Jesus and his mother of the gravest things.
rows.anchor: فرقة ترميه وحاشاه بأفظع ما رمت به أمه نبيها وهم أكثر اليهود

rows.speaker: العنانية
rows.claim: The Ananites, followers of Anan ben David, accept Jesus’s teachings and signs, say he upheld and preached the Torah as an Israelite worshipper, but deny that he was a prophet or messenger.
rows.anchor: العنانية أصحاب عنان بن داود رأس الجالوت

rows.speaker: العنانية
rows.claim: The Ananites say other Jews wronged Jesus by first disbelieving without understanding his claim and then killing him without understanding his purpose.
rows.anchor: العنانية أصحاب عنان بن داود رأس الجالوت

rows.speaker: العيسوية
rows.claim: The Isawiyya, followers of Abū ʿĪsā Isḥāq ibn Yaʿqūb al-Iṣfahānī, say a post-Mosaic messenger called the Messiah has not yet come; five messengers precede him, and their leader is one.
rows.anchor: العيسوية أصحاب أبي عيسى إسحاق بن يعقوب الاصفهاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī says these Jewish positions are far from the alleged claim, while allowing that its proponent may have found evidence unknown to him.
rows.anchor: وكل الأقوال بعيد عما ادعاه صاحب القيل بمراحل ولعله وجد ما يوافق دعواه ومن حفظ حجة على من لم يحفظ

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One account says Jesus received his mission in childhood, at three years old.
rows.anchor: فقيل : في الصبا وهو ابن ثلاث سنين

rows.speaker: البحر
rows.claim: Al-Baḥr says revelation came after Jesus reached adulthood, at age thirty, and that his prophethood lasted three years.
rows.anchor: وفي البحر : أن الوحي

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another reported chronology gives three months and three days before Jesus was raised to heaven; the source calls the age-thirty account famous.
rows.anchor: قيل : ثلاثة أشهر وثلاثة أيام ثم رفع إلى السماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source reports disagreement over whether Joseph or Moses was the first prophet of the Children of Israel, and identifies Jesus as the last.
rows.anchor: وفيه أن أول أنبياء بني إسرائيل يوسف وقيل : موسى وآخرهم عيسى

rows.speaker: اليزيدي
rows.claim: Al-Yazīdī reads “messenger” in the genitive, coordinating it with “a word.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ اليزيدي ورسولا بالجر على أنه معطوف على كلمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause “that I have come to you” is governed by “messenger,” which carries the sense of speaking.
rows.anchor: معمول لرسولا لما فيه معنى النطق

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ also allows the clause to modify “messenger,” to stand in apposition if messenger is a verbal noun, or to predicate an omitted noun phrase.
rows.anchor: أبو البقاء كونه معمولا لمحذوف وقع صفة لرسول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “With a sign” may be a circumstantial phrase meaning Jesus came bearing proof, or may attach to “I have come”; the bāʾ can mark accompaniment or transitivity.
rows.anchor: في موضع الحال أي محتجا أو متلبسا بآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite ending on “a sign” magnifies the sign rather than specifying that there was only one.
rows.anchor: والتنوين للتفخيم دون الوحدة لظهور ما ينافيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “From your Lord” may modify “sign” or “I have come”; in either case min marks figurative origination.
rows.anchor: في التقديرين لابتداء الغاية مجازا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address “your Lord” reinforces the duty to obey the coming commands and suits God’s role in sending Jesus to them.
rows.anchor: والتعرض لعنوان الربوبية مع الإضافة إلى ضمير المخاطبين لتأكيد إيجاب الامتثال لما سيأتي من الأوامر
